pack.name: Marketing
pack.title: The Whisper in the Aisle
pack.blurb: Brands, slogans, channels, pricing and the arts of persuasion.

prompts.flavor: You grew up with these names. They were in the pantry before you could read.
prompts.rules: Any brand that was founded in Australia or is best known as Australian, even if it is now foreign-owned.

answers.lore: Its jingle, recorded in 1938 by a seven-year-old, was at one time played on Sydney radio more than a hundred times a day.
The rotary clothes line Lance Hill welded up in his Adelaide backyard in 1945, from scrap tubing, so the washing would clear his wife's lemon tree.
A portable cooler, first sold in 1952 by Malley's of Sydney. The name became the Australian word for any cooler at all.

traps.reason: Sold here, and loved here, but founded somewhere else.

prompts.text: Name a brand name that people use as the everyday word for the thing.
prompts.flavor: The greatest victory a brand can win is also how it dies: its name becomes the word.
prompts.rules: Any trade mark, living or lapsed, that became the common name for a product or an action.

answers.lore: A trade mark of the Otis Elevator Company until 1950, when a US ruling found Otis's own advertisements had used it as an ordinary word.
An Australian brand of quilt from the 1970s. Elsewhere it is a duvet, but not here.
Registered as a trade mark in 1854 by Abraham Gesner, the Canadian geologist who first distilled it. From the Greek for wax.
A Bayer trade mark, launched in 1898 as a cough remedy and said to be non-addictive. Bayer lost the name, with Aspirin, after the First World War.
Trade-marked in 1925 by the DryIce Corporation of America for solid carbon dioxide. The company is gone. The name stayed.

traps.reason: That is the plain word. Give the brand name people say instead.
A famous brand, but nobody uses its name to mean the thing itself.

prompts.text: Name a social media platform or messaging app.
prompts.flavor: Something on the other side of the glass is learning what you like.
prompts.rules: Any social network, video or photo sharing platform, forum or messaging app, living or dead.

answers.lore: Three million users within months of launching in 2003. It turned down a 30 million dollar offer from Google, and was overtaken by Myspace within two years.
Launched in 1997 and usually called the first social network: profiles, friend lists and all. It closed in 2001, a few years too early.

traps.reason: Online, and enormous, but not a social network or a messaging app.

prompts.text: Name an advertising medium or marketing channel.
prompts.flavor: The message finds you on the road, in your pocket and in your sleep. It has many doors.
prompts.rules: Any place or way a business can put its message in front of customers.

answers.lore: Letters of smoke a kilometre high, first sold as advertising in 1922, when an RAF pilot wrote "Daily Mail" over the Epsom Derby.
The oldest broadcast medium there is. Criers called out a shopkeeper's wares in ancient Greece, and many Australian towns still appoint one.

traps.reason: Part of the plan, but not a channel that carries the message.

prompts.text: Name a pricing strategy or tactic.
prompts.flavor: The price was never about the cost. It was always about you.
prompts.rules: Any named way of setting, framing or changing a price.

answers.lore: A low headline price that grows as fees drip in before the checkout. The ACCC took Jetstar and Virgin to court over it in 2014, and won.
Same price, smaller packet. The word caught on in the 2010s. The Toblerone that grew wider gaps between its peaks in 2016 is the classic case.

traps.reason: The thing itself, not a strategy for setting it.
A different one of the four Ps.

prompts.text: Name a marketing concept, model or term.
prompts.flavor: They have a word for everything you feel in a shop. They had it before you felt it.
prompts.rules: Any idea, framework or piece of jargon from the study of marketing.

answers.lore: Being easy to think of and easy to find. The gospel of Byron Sharp at the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute in Adelaide, whose 2010 book upended brand theory.
Theodore Levitt's 1960 warning: the railways declined because they thought they were in the railway business, when they were in the transport business.

traps.reason: Business, yes, but not a marketing concept.

prompts.text: Name a fast food or restaurant chain.
prompts.flavor: The same sign on every highway in the world. You are never far from one. That is the idea.
prompts.rules: Any chain of fast food outlets, cafés or casual restaurants, Australian or overseas.

answers.lore: The all-you-can-eat salad bar and its cheese toast, beloved of Australian families from 1985. The last nine restaurants closed in November 2020.
An Adelaide seafood chain since 1970. South Australians will tell you it was the first drive-through in the country.

traps.reason: You can get food there, or through it, but it is not a restaurant chain.

prompts.text: Name a brand mascot or advertising character.
prompts.flavor: A smiling face with nothing behind it, built to be loved. It has been watching you since childhood.
prompts.rules: Any character invented to sell a product, a company or a cause. The brand's name counts if it is the character's name.

answers.lore: "Straight from rubbish tip to you." Drawn in 1957 for Mortein, with a jingle by a young copywriter named Bryce Courtenay, later Australia's best-selling novelist.
His real name is Bibendum, he is made of tyres, and he dates from 1898, when tyres were white. He once smoked cigars and drank nails and broken glass.
A square-jawed hero in a white singlet who ran as a newspaper comic strip from 1938 to 1964. It was among the first strips ever built around a product.

answers.answer: The Most Interesting Man in the World

traps.reason: A logo or a tune, not a character.
A character from a story. Mascots are born in the marketing department.
